speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Just before the House took recess at six o'clock, I stated, in answer to an ironical interruption by the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe), who seemed to take a sort of sarcastic pleasure in the use of the term "adequate protection," that the leader whom he will undoubtedly now support and the exMinister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) whom he supported for many years, proclaimed the Fielding tariff as a tariff of adequate protection. Now I propose to show that that is correct, and I do not think he was very far wrong in his description. In fact, in some cases I thought, and think still, he had too high protection. Speaking on the 7th of June, 1964, in the Budget Speech he said that his tariff had:
included a considerable measure of incidental protection-
That was the favourite word of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's all the time he was in office in describing his protective tariff. He took care almost universally to call it "incidental" protection, as if it made a bit of difference what adjective he applied to it, whether it was incidental, accidental or transcendental. It was not the adjective, but the amount of the duty that counted, and those who were interested in the tariff of Canada did not care whether he called it incidental protection or anything else. He went on to say:
-and in that respect It will command the admiration perhaps of hon. gentlemen opposite who are more anxious for protection than some of us on this side of the House.
"Same of us." He did not name them. He goes on:
X think as to whether or not it is adequate protection we have some evidence of a gratifying character that the tariff, without being excessive, is high enough to bring some American industries across the line-
Pretty real protection!

and a tariff which is able to bring these industries into Canada, looks very much like a tariff which affords adequate protection.
"Adequate protection."
And in the year 1909, I think it was or 1908, speaking on a motion for the further reduction of the duty on these very implements he made this statement, and I ask hon. gentlemen who feel like supporting the

hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's in this vague, visionary, misty, and cloudy resolution, after he has lopped off the specific and the actual, just to read what he said when in office and in which he still believes to-day, judging from, the whole tenor of his speech. Opposing the motion for reduction he said:
With a moderate duty we have induced American capital to come into Canada and to establish that great industry (The International Harvester Company of Hamilton) and after we have brought it in and established it in Canada, I believe that if we were to pass this resolution-
Reducing the duties, not making them free, but still leaving on 10 per cent. He says:
I believe that, if we were to pass this resolution the company operating that industry would find it profitable to close the Hamilton factory and bring in goods which they make in the United States.
That was his reason for oipposing the motion. He was opposed to reducing the duty by 7J. per cent when in office. But once out of office and when he wanted to perform a marriage ceremony with hon. gentlemen angularly opposite he is ready to take the whole duty off and leave it just as it w'as before 1896. He said:
On behalf of the Government I wish to say, following the statement of my hon. friend the Minister of Customs, that while we are not advocating a high tariff, while we are not advocating a Chinese wall tariff, while we are not seeking to shut everything out, we are willing that a moderate-
Listen to the words:
-that a moderate degree of protection, if you care to use the word, arising out of a tariff designed for revenue, but incidentally-
The same old phrase.
-giving some protection,-in some instances a considerable measure of protection-we are willing that, where there is a great industry in Canada, it shall receive a fair share of consideration which we have given by this tariff on agricultural implements, and so I must ask the House to reject the amendment of the hon. member for Souris.
Now it was argued in that debate, and argued again in the reciprocity debate in 1911, that the tariff that existed at that time, particularly the tariff on implements, was no more than a revenue tariff, and when the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's came back from Washington and announced his programme, he told the House that he could not reduce further the duty on implements, and he said that the reason was that to do so would be getting below the line of a revenue tariff. Now I ask hon. gentlemen
opposite if, at a time when the revenue necessities of this country were $125,000,000, the Fielding reciprocity tariff was no more than a revenue tariff, how does a much lower tariff become too high for a revenue tariff when the revenue necessities of this country are $350,000,000? Besides, through all those years, and many of them were hard years-there has never been a depression in Canada for twenty or thirty years like the depression of 1907 and 1908-he adhered to these means, and these means alone, of raising the revenue and never dared to impose one dollar of direct taxation in this country. I ask again if that Fielding tariff, if that scale of tariff, was no more than a revenue tariff, when we had not the courage to have direct taxation at all, how can hon. gentlemen complain of this scale now' that we have $81,000,000 by direct taxation and propose to have $181,000,000 next year? There could be nothing more inconsistent, nothing more ludicrously grotesque, than the position of hon. gentlemen opposite in respect of the scale of this tariff if they remember for one minute not only their owm innate beliefs on this subject, but the beliefs they put into practice through fifteen years of power.
Now I observe in this Liberal platform of August last, the greater part of which is now left at home, that they have changed the wrords of the farmers' resolution which calls for all foodstuffs to be put on the free list to read "the principal articles of food." The House will appreciate the skill of the generality, but would it not be interesting, and, indeed, is it not absolutely necessary, that the people of this country should know from hon. gentlemen opposite what these principal articles of food are. What are the principal articles of food? May I ask, is tea a principal article of food? I venture to say I shall never get an answrer from the leader of the Opposition, and I venture to say he will not give me an answer when he speaks in this debate. Is sugar a principal article of food? I would think it would be. We use something like $100,000,000 a year of sugar, we import $75,000,000, and we make quite a lot here. Is it the intention of hon. gentlemen opposite to put raw sugar and refined sugar on the free list? If it is, I think the country has a right to know. Whether it is their intention or not, I think the country has a right to know. Here is our tariff. What do you mean by your professions? Are meats a principal article of food? Are biscuits a principal article of food? Biscuits, the hallowred biscuits on which they never thought of revising the duty, even under reciprocity,

below 30 cents a pound. Are they a principal article of food? What are these principal articles of food? No answer, and there will be no answer, Mr. Speaker. It is in the vagueness and the generality of it that they take their refuge. Virtually all is vague and meaningless except the things that are free now, that were put in for mere padding, to make an appearance, and to paint a little ornament to look like the Farmers' platform. I have not succeeded in getting much in the way of answer from the leader of the Opposition.
He has not been given an opportunity to reply.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. leader of the Opposition will have his opportunity in due course.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: If any hon. gentleman has a remark to make he might do the House the courtesy of rising in his seat.
I rise to a point of order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
What is the point of
order?

My point of order is,
Sir, that by your ruling we are precluded from the possibility of answering questions asked by the member who has the floor.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I fail to observe the
point of order. The hon. member who has raised it has trifled with the rules of order of the House, which are clear and distinct. A question may be submitted by an hon. member who has the floor but no member has any right to make any statement in reply, even with the consent of the hon. member who has the floor.

It was just a figure
of rhetoric.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It has been the practice that an hon. gentleman, with the consent of the member who has the floor, may reply. I do not wish to question the ruling of the Chair, but I want to add this, that no hon. member has been precluded from replying to any question by any act of mine, either on this or on any other occasion. In fact, I should be pleased if the rule of the House could be ignored so far as this point is concerned.
Now, I desire to refer to one thing else, and it is clearly in harmony with the whole proceeding we are witnessing now. Hon. members will recall that a leading figure in the Liberal Convention in August last was the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding). Not satisfied with

the result of his labours, and no doubt having some recollection of the agony he went through in 1896 and the humiliating position in which he was frequently placed thereafter, he went back and wrote in the Journal of Commerce, a paper which he edits in the city of Montreal, a clear intimation, which I can read to the House if it desires, that the only practical acceptation of the platform of hon. gentlemen opposite was one with "interpretations and reservations," and that anyway platforms that were made at conventions were made in a hurry and were not footstools of policy or declarations of principle, but were merely in the nature of platforms on Pullman coaches to get in upon. That is the frank confession of the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's, and this platform which he himself denominated as a mere means to get in on is the platform of which he takes a truncated section and brings it into this House seeking by so doing to get a vote of want of confidence against the Government.
I remarked a few moments ago that we never had even from hon. gentlemen of the Agrarian party any motion in this House asking this House to debate and declare its judgment upon the platform which they profess. A year, or two years ago-I forget which -we had an attempt on the part of the hon. member for Red Deer to bring in something of the kind. It was stated at that time by you, Mr. Speaker, that on a motion to go into Ways and Means, that is to say, on the Budget debate, one amendment could be moved and no sub-amendment could be moved thereto, and also that, no second amendment could be moved after the first amendment had been defeated. In other words, there can be only one amendment. Hlon. gentlemen knew that right well. It was shown them clearly by Mr. Speaker two years ago. But they come to this debate with a motion in amendment made by the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's, a member of the official Opposition; and members of the Agrarian party know that by allowing him to make this motion they are precluded from moving their platform by way of amendment. Why was that? Was a request made that they be allowed to move their platform by way of amendment, and was it refused? I think not. Is i't not clearly the purpose to protect those hon. gentlemen opposite from declaring where they stand on the farmers' platform? The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) laughs. For two years, or for something more than

one year at any rate, the hon. gentleman has been a private member, and neither he nor any of his followers has ever put that platform on the Orders of the Day. They have never sought a discussion of it in this House; they have never challenged the opinions of hon. members in regard to it; they have never put hon. gentlemen opposite in the position of voting Yea or Nay. They have left them in such a position that they can go hand in hand with themselves in the country never having come into a recorded antagonism in Parliament. Each side can hold up a different flag and follow a different leader, seeking to get the free trade vote in one part of Canada and the protectionist vote in another, and then afterwards come back together to show the people of the country just what they care for the opinions and professions they make before a contest. That was the performance in 1897. It looks as if something even worse were on the programme to-day, and I am confirmed in that statement by the opinions freely and definitely expressed on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite. I know that the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Beland) went to Montreal to the sanctuary of Liberalism, the Reform club, and stated there at. the time of the by-election in St. James, that he did not stand for free trade; that, in fact, there was not a single free trader in his party. He said he stood for a well-regulated system of protection. And the hon. member now for St. James (Mr. Rinfret) declared in his speech in that campaign that he too stood for the encouragement of industries by a protective system. He was elected, not on the platform that is here moved in amendment, not on anything that bears a family resemblance to the professions of hon. gentlemen in the Agrarian party. He was elected on the platform upon which this Government stands in regard to tariff matters. That, Sir, is what he was elected on. He utilizes the tariff policy of this Administration to get elected in order afterwards to vote a want of confidence in the Government that puts forward that policy. That is his position.
Why did you not get him elected?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Well, he got elected and the man on the other side stood for the same. As between the two, there was not much difference so far as we were concerned; and all we ask of the hon. member for St. James is that he now vote according to the professions he made, that he stand true to the electors to whom he made those
professions, on the strength of which he got their votes. And what about the hon. member for Huntingdon (Mr. Robb)? He too was in the Montreal Reform Club and made a speech in which he defined himself as clearly in favour of the encouragement of the industries of a country by legislation. That is where he stands. And what about the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. Pardee) who represents the city of Sarnia and the thriving county of Lambton? He went to the same Montreal Reform Club and he denounced free trade hip and thigh. He declared himself in favour of a tariff not only for the purpose of revenue but because we had to have a tariff for economic reasons, for protective reasons, and he knows he stands for that principle. He knows he is an advocate of protection as a principle; he would not dare to vote for a resolution in this House, that denounced the principle of protection. Now I ask him if in this debate, where there is nothing at all in controversy but that principle, to stand up and vote as he professes and believes.
We have all these declarations of faith on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite saying to the people of Eastern Canada to its farthest limits " Do not be afraid of us. Here is our faith presented by Mr. Pardee of Lambton, Mr. Rinfret of St. James, Mr. Beland of Beauce, Mr. Robb of Huntingdon, and Mr. Lemieux" -they might just as well add him and they could add fifty more-" here is our faith, do not be afraid of us, vote for us on a policy of moderate protection." At the same time we have hon. gentlemen across the way saying in Western Canada " vote for us as free traders pure and simple, seeking free trade with United States, and with Great Britain first, and then with all the world." Then we have the leader-who hopes to be the leader of both parties if they get into power-trying to sing a song that attunes with each, and telling the people in all ends of Canada that the Liberal party and the Liberal platform are, to all intents and purposes, the same as 'the farmers' party and the farmers' platform. That is to say that protection and free trade are to all intents and purposes the same. The one principle is the profession of my hon. friends opposite, the other principle is the profession of hon. gentlemen on the cross benches; and the leader (Mr. King) claiming them both as his own in order to pave the way for the great betrayal when the day comes, if it ever comes, that their

united numbers are greater than the numbers behind the present Government.
Now I stated a moment ago that in this country to-day we had not anything in the nature of an immoderate tariff. It may be -it doubtless is the case-that there are portions of that tariff that can be scaled down, that upon investigation it will be seen that deductions can be made. There may be other changes that may be necessary. The principle upon which the revision will be made is clear and well defined and all understand it. It will be designed to keep industries in Canada, to enable industries to expand, but wTill go no further than is essential for that purpose when accompanied by competent business management. Now surely that principle is plain. Will the hon. member for Quebec East (Mr. Lapointe) say he could not support a tariff designed for that purpose and with that restraint? He could not say so. Why do not hon. gentlemen who believe in the principle I am expounding and who know this tariff is true to that principle-why do they not support it? Just in order that a political manoeuvre may be played and for no other reason whatsoever.
We have direct taxation now in this country, and the Government that imposed it is the Government in office. The Government that took all the responsibility and unpopularity of imposing direct taxation, that is the Government that new appeals to this House of Commons. The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar), the great champion of direct taxation, who has been preaching it in season and out of season all over this country, votes against the Government of direct taxation. He votes for hon. gentlemen opposite who never introduced the policy of direct taxation, and he holds the sheltering hand of his protection over Provincial Governments that do not put on the direct taxation that he advocates. Let us now have an examination into the policy of the hon. member. He says "I want to do away with custom duties." That is what he tells the people of the West,-do away with them. "It is no way in the world," he says, "to raise a revenue." "It is the most costly wray'' is the way he expresses in Brandon "ever devised by man."
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
"Hear, hear," the hon. gentleman says to-day; he says: put in its place income tax, a graduated income tax, and a tax on the unearned increment of land. That is his statement. His platform

does not call for a tax on the unearned increments of land but for a tax on the unimproved value of land, a different thing altogether. However, I want the House to know that those are his two main substitutes. The others are purely provincial taxes, inheritance and the like-those first are the two main substitutes the hon. gentlemen advocates-land tax, and income tax. Now I hold in my hands the report of a tax commission appointed by the Government of Manitoba, the Government which is very close to the hon. member for Marquette, and whose continuance in office is one of the things dearest to his heart. I am not saying anything against that Government at the present time, that is not an issue in this debate; I am saying something about the consistency of the hon. member. That Government appointed a commission, and so far as I know a commission of pretty able men, to go into the question of this taxation and to report to the administration. That commission was composed of, I think, ten or a dozen men. There were represented on it the farmers of Manitoba, representatives of the rural councils of that province. Other interests in Manitoba were also represented, and among them the actual Grain Growers Association that is the very party that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Crerar) champions and leads in this House. They were directly represented on that commission by two men. Of these, one, Mr. Peter Wright, is a director of the Canadian Council of Agriculture, is he not?
One of the directors.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: One of the directors of the Canadian Council of Agriculture, the council that propounded this Farmers' platform, and Mr. W. Wood is the secretary of the Farmers' party in Manitoba. Now the commission examined into this land tax, it examined into the income tax, it examined into single tax, and all other taxes; it reported against single tax in the most decisive terms. On discussing the merits of the land tax, a tax on land of any kind-on unimproved land or an unearned increment tax-it decided that a tax on land was a good thing by local authorities for local purposes but that a tax on land was a bad thing for the federal authorities for any purpose at all. 1 have the very words of that report in front of me.
Did Messrs. Wright and Wood sign that report?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Wright signed the report. Mr. Wood did not sign the report

but he made no minority report. I have the -report before me and Mr. Wright's signature appears thereon. Here is what they say about the land tax:
There are accordingly several cogent reasons why the taxation of real property has tended more and more to become the special prerogative of the local authorities. For the Dominion Government in this country, for example, to encroach on the field of real property taxation would, in the light of both history and theory, be a distinctly retrograde step.
And that is one of the taxes that the Farmers' party led by the hon. member for Marquette says that we should adopt, that is one of the fields he says we should invade which the Manitoba Government commission unanimously find-every man who signs the report finds-to be debarred by its own nature from adoption by the federal authorities for any purpose. Then they go on to the income tax, and what do they say about it? I am sorry that the hon. member for Bed Deer is not here. This would be very interesting to that hon. member who complains of the small amount of income tax collected from the farmers. The commission quote with approval what Professor Adams says:
The income tax yields little or no revenue in rural or farming districts, and for that reason I would not recommend it to farming comtnuri-ties; but for thickly settled manufacturing and urban communities, it is bound to spread and in the end to supplant the relatively unjust and unfair tax on personal property.
This seems to toe the prevailing opinion everywhere.
Tn the income tax provisions of the province of Ontario we find that the income of fanners derived from the produce of their farms is expressly exempted from taxation under the income tax law.
We have carefully and fully considered this feature, and recommend that the provisions of any general income law that may be enacted in this province, be confined wholly and exclusively to urban communities.
It is to be borne in mind that the application of a provincial income tax to the farmer would, in any event, be lost energy, in that, if such were imposed, and the amount derived in each municipality was returned to the source derived, it would be equivalent to travelling north by south.
There is the report of this commission unanimously adopted and concurred in by a director of the Canadian Council of Agriculture, Mr. Peter Wright. Mr. Peter Wright is a man for whose opinion and personality I have the profoundest respect. He is a man who has rendered splendid service in our soldier settlement work. Mr. Peter Wright, after investigation, signs that report and says that, of the substitute taxes which the hon. member 172
for Marquette proposes to take the place of the customs tax, the land tax is one we should not adopt and that the income tax is all right so long as we do not touch the farmers of Canada. I will ask the hon. member for Marquette-I will not ask hilm to reply now but I will be happy if he will reply when he takes his feet: Does he propose to repudiate Mr. Peter Wright who has gone into this case and got the evidence, and who is a director of his own association, and one of the framers of its platform, or does he propose to change his policy?
I stated to the House that the tax on large incomes in England was lower than in Canada. This is interjected out of its place because I did not have the figures before me then. I stated that the turning point was about incomes of $200,000. I have been sent over from the Finance Department the figures which give the tax on incomes of $100,000, $500,000 and up to $1,000,000. I do not have the figures for an income of $200,000, but I think that is about the turning point. The tax on incomes of $500,000 in Canada, under last year's scale, is $303,190. The tax on the same income in the United States is exactly the same amount. The tax on the same income in Great Britain is $257,321, or almost $50,000 less than the. tax that we collect in Canada.
Would the hon. gentleman give the tax on an income of $100,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
An income of $100,000 is more heavily taxed in England, and so are smaller incomes all down the line. The tax on an income of $100,000 in Canada is $31,190 and in the United States the same. In England the tax is $47,327. Coming to the incomes of $1,000,000, our tax is $663,190 while the British tax is $519,812.77, or a difference of almost $150,000, between the tax on a million-dollar income in England and in Canada. Yet, we are upbraided-upbraided, it is true, for political purposes and no other- by hon. gentlemen opposite who say we are protecting the rich man and the millionaire and that we ought to follow the example of England. Our tax with respect to all these cases of high income is emphatically higher than in England, it is higher than in Australia, higher than in that paradise of income taxation referred to by the hon. member foT Red Deer, New Zealand. Their tax on an income of $1,000,000 is $374,993- away below ours; and on an income of $500,000 it is $187,496 or very little more than half the tax in Canada.



I have sought to show that the tariff as now proposed should remain in effect pending a thorough revision, which, hon. gentlemen opposite admit could not have been made up to the present time. The hon. member for Red Deer clearly admitted that. This is the tariff, and not higher, but lower than that adopted by hon. gentlemen opposite when they were in office under circumstances of far less urgent need. It is admitted to be a tariff which is lower than that which hon. gentlemen opposite unanimously supported all through those fifteen years. It is a tariff not designed to benefit the rich in this country; it is designed, s* far as our own information goes-and it cannot be complete without investigation only to give such measure of assistance ar to retain within this country its industrial strength, and which does not alienate from this country a measure of the industrial strength that we have. We never can have a high tariff in Canada. We cannot have a high tariff in Canada for the most obvious reasons. In the first place, a high tariff is unsound in principle in that it tendto eliminate one of the factors of competition, namely, foreign goods. Foreign goods should be allowed to enter into competition under fair conditions in this or in any other country. But the conditions under free trade or without protection are such that the foreign competitor has every advantage.
Take an illustration. Here is a foreign competitor in the United States competing with the manufacturer in England. Are the conditions equal? Is a man in the United States, where he can get the biggest concern, the biggest industrial unit, the biggest output, in the same position as the man in England? He can have a much larger unit. He has a market of 110,000,000 assured to him right at home that no government can take awTay. In Great Britain he has another market of 43,000,000 almost at hand and free of access to him. He has the same show exactly as the British manufacturer in all the other countries of the world. He therefore has a free market of 153,000,000 to sell his output to. Where is his British competitor? What is his position?	He has the bars up against
him in the United States; he cannot get into that market save over the tariff wall. He has the same restrictions against him in other countries of the world and all he has left to him is that portion of his own home market of 43,000,000 that may be uninvaded by the products of other lands. Is that equal competition? Bring similar conditions here and you would soon paralyze and destroy the whole

industrial fabric of this country. So I say we cannot have any immoderate or high tariff for the reason, first, that it tends to exclude that healthy element of fair conditions, namely, foreign competition; secondly, we have in Canada a territory of wide extent. We have one portion of Canada, newer than the other portion, a more predominatingly agricultural country, newer to manufactures and industrial development, and consequently the advantages of the tariff do not accrue to them as yet as they ultimately will accrue to them. They come more immediately to one portion of this country than to another. On account of these two reasons we must always have in this country nothing more than a moderate tariff under any conditions whatsoever. That will be the purpose of the revision, under the principles clearly set out, enunciated by the Minister of Finance, to which we adhere. On that policy I appeal to hon. gentlemen who have something great or small at stake in this Dominion- yes, I appeal to citizens, men and women who have nothing of this world's goods at stake, whose only concern is the well-being of their native land. There are those among us who will not see with their eyes or hear with their ears or understand with their hearts; there is that class in Canada, as in England, and there always will be in every country. I cannot appeal to those to whom experience has taught nothing and for whom reason has no persuasion. But to all others who will thoroughly study the needs of Canada; who will thoroughly study the example of other nations, and most of all, the example of the Mother Country herself-I appeal to them to yield support to what is fair and right. Come what may, good or ill fortune, I prefer to be of the number of those who have stood loyally by clear and well-defined and well-tried principles, who have been loyal to them in office and out of office, rather than among those who have two policies, one to profess and the other to practice.

speakeroldname: Mr. M. J. DEMERS (fit. Johns and Iberville) :
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will not intervene in the contest between the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) and the member for Red Deer (Mr. Clark), because I admit I am not big enough to throw any light upon the question, for instance, whether the balance of trade should be considered in connection with the fiscal policy to be adopted by any country. I must say that after the speech of the Minister of the Interior I am more than ever in the dark as to that question of balance of trade. He told the House

that 'Germany and the United States were prosperous with a balance of trade in their favour, and that England was prosperous with an adverse balance of trade. This question has been an open one for centuries; I think that it will continue so for some few centuries to come.
The Minister of the Interior read to the House lengthy quotations from the report of a commission appointed to study economic conditions in England. The fact remains that since that report was submitted in 1918 nothing has been done to comply with the findings of the majority of the commissioners. We all know that many by-elections have since been held in England, and I do not think that the electors there approved in any shape or form of the changes proposed in that report.
I wish to refer to what the Minister of the Interior said in respect to a statement made by the member for Antigonish and Guys-borougn (Mr. Sinclair). He said that the Auditor General's Report is open to revision and investigation by the Public Accounts Committee. I would like to remind the minister that the volume containing the particular item in question was brought down only last week, so we have had no time to take it up before the Public Accounts Committee.
The question before the House is a very important one. The ground has been pretty well covered since the beginning of this debate, but there are certain matters upon which I desire to express my views. I listened with interest to the speech of the Minister of Finance, which has been awaited with curiosity, I may say with anxiety. I was disappointed in it, because I found that the most important problem that confronts us, the cost of living, had not received the least consideration from this Government. I was disappointed to a certain degree, but not to the extent of being surprised, because it is well known that the Government have done absolutely nothing to bring relief to the consumers who have suffered and are still suffering to the extent of depriving themselves of certain necessities of life. All that the Government did on that account was to create a body known as the Board of Commerce, which, in my judgment, was an absolute failure. It will be said, I know, that the problem of the cost of living is a very difficult one. We all know that; but we all know also that it is not a more difficult problem in this country than it is in other countries. We know what has been done in some other countries, and we can appreciate the good results of the drastic
m*
measures which have elsewhere been taken against profiteers. The effect of the application of these measures, Mr. Speaker, was magic; to-day we witness a real race in the United States in the lowering of prices. England as well has taken action to fight profiteers and the high cost of living; the same is true of France and many other countries. Here we have had investigations which have shown how we have been oppressed by the profiteers in connection with the necessaries of life. It has been established that canners and packers and proprietors of refrigerating plants are madnljy responsible for the increase in the price of foodstuffs. To my mind, it would have been easy to check them by a proper and strict control of their operations and by the enactment of laws providing stern punishment for unreasonable profiteering. The Government have been warned again and again without success. Notwithstanding the negligence of the Government in that regard to date, the people of this country were expecting an announcement of some measures of relief on the occasion of the presentation of the Budget. They expected that the production of foodstuffs would be stimulated by the removal of customs duties from agricultural implements and the necessaries of life generally. They, however, failed to see anything of the kind in the speech of the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton), and their only comfort is to learn that the Government need money and that the people will be called upon to pay the bill. Increased taxes all along-that is the only relief offered to the people in the critical situation in which we are. We all admit that Canada must meet her obligations and that for that purpose the Government must levy taxes; but the reproach that we have to make to the Government is that we are called upon to pay for extravagances and waste, and also to pay our war debt when that war debt should have been paid during the war and since by the war profiteers and not by the whole community.
The other day the Minister of Finance spoke about economy. We can hardly reconcile the strong plea he made the other day for economy with the Estimates of $12,000,000 for military expenses. We cannot share the hopes of the Minister of Finance for the future of this country when we consider the shipbuilding policy of the Government. We cannot hope for financial success in the future when we consider the railway policy of this Government. I am not a pessimist, but for me to become an optimist would require a change of Gov-

ernment. If the ministers of the Cabinet are anxious to do something for the good of the country, let them dissolve Parliament. This is the wish of the people-of farmers, soldiers, labourers and consumers-and nobody can deny that. The people are not satisfied that we were elected in normal times and by normal means, and they believe that we received only a war-time mandate, because that mandate was given in a war-time election. Why should the Government accentuate uneasiness, discontent and indignation, by refusing to comply with the general and obvious desire of the people?
The Minister of Finance is standing by protection or by what is called generally the "National Policy." I am glad that this opportunity is afforded to me to express my views on the economic question as regards this country. I am not a protectionist; I stand for the Liberal platform of 19X9 as enunciated at the Liberal convention, I am for a tariff for revenue. I want to speak frankly. If I had been in politics in 1878, I would have opposed the so-called National Policy, and I believe the situation and1 the conditions of the country in 1896, after eighteen years of that regime, would have justified my calculations.
The National Policy led the country to the verge of bankruptcy; it created large fortunes for a few privileged people; but it was detrimental to the great majority of the people of Canada. I am opposed to the so-called National Policy, although I must admit that in the framing of a fiscal policy for this country, we must take into consideration actual conditions as they were produced by such a policy. In 1893, the Liberal party pronounced itself in favour of the principle of greater freedom of trade, and to-day, the party is charged with not having fulfilled its promises in this respect. Every day we hear that the fiscal policy of the Liberal party when in power was the same as that of the Conservative party, and opponents of the Liberal party are naturally interested in trying to create that impression. It seems as if they fail to remember the great fiscal modifications brought about by the Laurier Government; they seem to forget that the Laurier Government lowered the customs duties on about 150 articles of the tariff and abolished the duties on many other articles of the tariff. They would not admit the real endeavour of the party to apply its principles, and in their appreciation of the fiscal policy of the Liberal party, they fail to take into consideration the fact that we had in this country during eighteen years previously to 1896, a regime
fM. Demers. 1
of high protection. Was the Liberal party wheen it came into power to act by revolution or by evolution? The wisdom of the leaders induced them to choose the way of moderation and good order, and the party moved on gradually towards its aim, succeeding in reaching the reciprocity treaty of 1911. The fiscal policy of the Liberal party from 1896 to 1911 has been such that not one of its followers with lower-tariff tendencies thought it necessary to withdraw his allegiance from his party during the fifteen years of the Liberal administration. There were some Liberals who left the party because of its fiscal policy, but only those who were high protectionists. It is unfair to say that there is no difference between the Liberal and the Tory fiscal policies, for everybody knows that the Liberal party fell in 1911 in trying to put its principles of a low tariff into effect. There is absolutely no justification for saying that there is no difference between the two parties when not only were promises made but the Reciprocity Treaty was effected between the United States and iCanada. In view of that treaty,
I can hardly forgive those who persist in saying there is no difference between the Liberal and the Tory party fiscal policies.
It is not worthy, it seems to me, for a public man to appear not to appreciate the differ- , ence that does exist between the two parties. The Liberal party stands by its principles. We have not changed. More than ever we believe that the application of a tariff for revenue should be the fiscal policy of this country, and that considerable reductions should be made in the tariff in the interests of the welfare and prosperity of this country.
With protection we have created large cities, but that policy has been detrimental to the farming community. Our country is mainly agricultural, and instead of establishing a policy the effect of which was to bring into the cities our young men of the country, I think it would have been far better to concentrate our energies on the development of our agricultural industry. For my part I would prefer Montreal with a population of 300,000 men and the other 300,000 on the farms, because I would be sure then that that other 300,000 would be engaged in the production of the first necessities of life. Agriculture is our principal natural resource. By high protection it has been deprived of the labour it requires to such a degree that a very serious problem has been created and is facing us at the present time. I have no hesitation in saying that because of the shortage of farm labour

our farms are producing only about half of what they could produce. This is the direct result of high protection, and we must face the situation. We must do something to improve our agricultural industry. I regret that there is nothing substantial to be found in the Budget to help relieve conditions in this vital industry. The Finance Minister should have immediately decided on the free admission of agricultural implements, and should have reached the conclusion that the Reciprocity Treaty of 1911 should be revived. The minister gives us a promise of tariff revision, but can we take his declaration as a certainty or even as a probability after the promise we had last year from another Minister of Finance of this same administration? The Finance Minister, however, has spoken of having a revision of the tariff. If such a revision ever takes place let us hope that its principle will be a tariff for revenue without a vestige of protection, for protection means privilege. We have made immense sacrifices in the past to establish the industries of this country, some of which were what I might call exotics; that is, they had to get all their materials from other countries. Some of them now are very prosperous indeed, and, due to the fact that the Government has given them such high protection, we have witnessed the scandalous spectacle of some of these industries selling their products cheaper in Europe than in Canada. I say, let these industries take care of themselves now that they are strong, and if they are to receive any protection out of the tariff, let that protection be only incidental. If we had given to agriculture the protection that has been given to other industries what a prosperous and happy population would be ours to-day. If we had had more solicitude and paid more attention to the development of our natural industries, such as mines, pulp, paper, furniture and all those industries using lumber or iron and steel as their raw materials, we would certainly have had a much more prosperous country to-day and a more contented and a happier people.
Those are my views on the fiscal question. I shall leave to other hon. members to answer the arguments of the Minister of the Interior specifically, because there are answers to give. I have given my reasons for favouring a tariff strictly for revenue, that is to say, the establishment of customs duties in order to get the money necessary for the good administration of this country.

speakeroldname: Mr. EDGAR KEITH SPINNEY (Yarmouth and Claire) :
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have hesitated in engaging in the debate on the very important subject now before the House, feeling that both the hon. members of this House and the public generally were already over-fed by the conflicting views expressed by hon. members.
May I be permitted, Sir, first to join with many other members of this House in extending to the hon. Minister of Finance (Six Henry Drayton) my very hearty congratulations on the great care and honesty of purpose , he has displayed in preparing his Budget, and on his clear and lucid manner of presenting it to this Parliament. His declaration of the huge debt confronting this country shows no disposition to suppress the ghastly facts.
While it is not my purpose to refer at any length to the horrors of the atrocious war which convulsed the nations of the world, and in which Canada was so deeply involved, I cannot permit this occasion to pass without giving expression to our deep gratitude to our brave soldiers who so courageously and promptly obeyed the call to arms in defence of liberty, justice and democracy-three principles for which all Canadians in conjunction with other portions of this great Empire stand. Their services are far beyond commercial value, as the enjoyment of our liberty to-day is due to their great bravery and valour in conjunction with the army of the Allies.
We are also proud as Canadians of the hearty co-operation of all our people in that crisis by their willing and generous response in providing the adequate funds necessary in the successful carrying out of that great war. I desire especially to pay a high tribute to the women of Canada who took so prominent a part in this important movement. They indeed set a good examlple to the sterner sex in the great sacrifices they made and in the successful efforts they achieved in connection with Red Cross work and in their constant endeavours to send comfort to our noble soldiers in the trenches. We can well say, from the depths of our hearts, God bless the women of Canada.
While the penalty of this terrible conflict from a financial standpoint is great, yet it has no comparison with the loss involved When, approximately, 60,000 of our brave soldiers were called upon to pay the supreme sacrifice. Our hearts go forth in deep sympathy to those who were called upon to mourn the loss of their near and dear ones. The sacrifice of these valuable lives to this nation cannot be estimated or overcome.

(Translation) : Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in the discussion on the Budget, I do not intend to retain the attention of the House for a long criticism of what the honourable ministers and the honouiaible members sitting to your right may have said. Moreover, in spite of their great speeches, as far as I am concerned, the situation is always the same. The Union Government, which was born in the midst of prejudices and racial divisions, and constituted for the sole purpose of winning the elections, never had any other fiscal policy that that of the old Tory party.

Hear,
hear.

When it was formed, the Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) had intended, by calling a few Liberals into his Government, to make the people believe that the principles of the two great political parties were equally represented in the new Cabinet. But to-day, Mr. Speaker, when three so-called Liberal ministers have resigned and have jiot been replaced, and when, on a total of fifteen ministers, there are but four left who are supposed to be Liberals, can it be claimed that the Liberal party is really represented? I say supposed Liberals, because one cannot seriously believe that the honourable President of the Council (Mr. Rowell), the hon. Minister of Immigration (Mr. Calder), the honourable Solicitor General (Mr. Guthrie), and the honourable Secretary of State (Mr. Sifton) do represent the Liberal idea in the Cabinet; so much so, that not a single one of the four gentlemen whom I have mentioned could get elected in any division of the country as a Liberal, and, Mr. Speaker, you are well aware of the fact that, long ago, they have sacrificed their
political principles to retain their portfolios as ministers. Therefore, it is not to be wondered at that the Government should wish to maintain its protection policy. May I be permitted, Mr. Speaker, to say right away, that I have no confidence in the protection which had no other effect (than to enrich a certain class and to keep the people in a condition of hardship.

Hear,
hear.

I want
the tariff to be lowered. I believe in the Liberal platform which was accepted at the great convention of August last, and where every province and every class was represented; I have confidence in that platform, I believe that when it is put into effect, it twill bring comfort to this country and will restore peace within its limits; we shall, then, hear no more of the uneasiness now prevailing among the workingmen, or of any United Farmers' party, because the Liberal flag is wide enough to shelter all the groups under its folds; it wilt satisfy the workingmen by lowering the cost of living, by doing away with the middlemen and the trusts who are growing rich at the expense of the people; it will satisfy the farmers by abolishing the duties on the. farming implements and on all that which is necessarily required for a greater production.
Sir, I said that protection is the policy of the Government. That is so true that for two years they have been promising a readjustment of the tariff without ever redeeming their pledge. During the first session of 1919, I remember, the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White), who was also Acting Prime Minister, only succeeded in placating his supporters by stating in the House that a committee would be named at once to travel around the country and revise the tariff. Over a year has passed away since then and nothing has been performed yet, and this year, facing the same wranglings among his supporters, the present Minister of Finance attempted to make the same promise, but the trick had been detected and the remedy was not as efficient. Having been deceived last year by the former Minister of Finance, they demanded the pledge of the real Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden). But it was a serious, a very serious matter to disturb the Prime Minister who was sick, who had left a year ago for distant lands in order to recuperate. True it is that the press informed us now and then that he was recovering,

Dont
forget the profiteers.

Mr. Speaker I would never finish if I were to recite all the instances of extravagance on the part of the present Government, an extravagance only too plainly revealed to-day by the taxes saddled on the country. Who will be taxed to pay for all the boards of enquiry appointed for the sole purpose of paying swollen salaries to political friends? Of what benefit were all these commissions? What did they do to decrease the cost of living? Absolutely nothing, Mr. Speaiker; instead they were perhaps instrumental in furnishing the -profiteers with information which helped them to mulct the people even more.
And thus increase the cost of living.

This year we are going to spend millions on a standing army doubled since the conclusion of peace. During the war, in which we had such a glorious share, we were told in this House that all these sacrifices were necessary to encompass the defeat of Prussian militarism. Having seen the strength of our standing army doubled, having heard

certain hon. members on the other side of the House call upon the Government to establish compulsory military service, haven't we the right, Mr. Speaker, to conclude that the Government wants to set up militarism in Canada?
No.

So much
the better, then. Isn't the Government mocking those who gave their lives for a cause that was dear to them and who to-day are sleeping the glorious sleoip of sacrificed heroes? Isn't it mockery in the face of the people of Canada to spend their gold foT the establishment in this country of a system they gave their blood to destroy beyond the sea?
Either militarism is a good thing or it is not. If it be a good thing, Mr. Speaker, I wonder why we made such tremendous sacrifices to accomplish its downfall in Europe; and if it he a had thing I am at a loss to understand the Governments efforts to bring it into being in this country.
The hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken), whom I congratulate on his eloquent speech the other day, told ns how he became converted to toTyism. He told us that his father was a Liberal and that he himself had been a Liberal up to the time when he was 21 years of age; according to the hon. member, when he was 21 neither party was any good and, since he could do no worse he voted for Sir John A. Macdonald. That is the only reason he gave this House for his political conversion. It appears to me that the hon. member would have great difficulty in finding a worse Government than the one we have to-day and he would1 he perfectly justified in declining to oppose any longer those who sit on your left, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member for West Toronto, whose absence from the Chamber I notice with regret, spoke of the tremendous saving effected by the Government in letting out 300 employees of the Printing Bureau; however, if I remember correctly, we voted last year something like $500,000 to replace these 300 employees. I can't say that I find that veTy much of a saving. If the hon. member is of the opinion that the Government saved a lot of money by letting out 300 employees he will likely be scandalized to learn that this same Government has taken on 27,000 new employees since the end of the war.
As a consequence of such a policy we behold our young country to-day carrying a eolassal burden of taxes on all the necessaries of life.
[ Mr. Fafard.]
Those who raise a numerous family destined to furnish the country with valuable hands to insure production, will pay four or five times more taxes than the others.
I am in favour of taxing luxuries, but I do not consider that, at this time, a $9 pair of hoots or a $45 suit of clothes are articles of luxury. -, Nothing in the preparation of this budget has 'been done to decrease the high cost of giving.
Hoarders fill their storehouses with enormous quantities of goods in order to bring about a rise in the prices. There is, at this moment, more sugar in the Canadian warehouses than there has ever been. The Government knows this, and it would be very easy to have a law permitting inspectors to go and visit suoh warehouses, and obliging the hoarders to put upon the market at current prices the commodities with which they are stocked, causing a rise in the cost of living. But the Government protects these profiteers at the expense of the public.
If you read the Budget carefully, Mr. Speaker-even though you will have heard a lot about ito-you will find that two classes only have not been taxed. You might believe at first blush that one of them is the (Soldiers that have returned from the front ,and of whom we heard so much during the war; but no, these soldiers, foi the Government supporters, are an interest of the past. Their praise iwas on their lips during the war; but no, these soldiers, for the Govern-one of the members who sit on your right .will he willing to give them any credit. If we are to judge from their utterances in this House, it is evident that it was they and not the soldiers who won the war. _
The only two classes of persons or things, which escaped taxing are the profiteers and ithe orders in council.

Hear,
hear.

A revision of (the tariff would have had a good effect on the cost of living and would have reduced it. Nothing was done. I say that in order to decrease the cost of living, and towards (furthering the general good of the country, a revision of the tariff is imperative at the present moment. The Government have no aright to overburden the people with taxes jn order to allow there favorites to build colossal fortunes. These favorites are but a few while the consumer is the whole people. In a democratic country, all the citizens

should he equal and enjoy the same privileges.
The hon. members of the right seem to believe that the fact of our favouring a decrease of the tariff shows a desire to ruin industry. A lowering of the tariff Would have altogether another effect. The result would be manufacturing in larger quantities, as well as an increase in the revenue of the country.
It does not require to be an expert, but a little good will is sufficient, to understand that it is not so much the high rate of duty which piles up revenue as the quantity of goods coming through the customs. If you add to the tariff on certain articles, the present rate of exchange, you will find it altogether prohibitive.
Everybody complains, and justly, of the high cost of living and of the dearness of food. The cost of articles of food, as of the other commodities, varies according to the law of supply and demand, and it is evident to any observer that, since the war, the equilibrium has been destroyed.
When two workmen come to an employer and ask for work, it is the employer who fixes the pay; but when two employers seek the labour of one workman, it is the workman who settles the price. What is true in one case is true in the other. When there are ten workmen that are consumers to one farmer who produces, it is the farmer who fixes prices, and when there are ten farmers producing to one workman to consume, it is the workman who decides what shall be paid. Hence, I come to the conclusion that, for the last few years, our industries, owing to protection, have gone on at a faster rate-too fast even-at a faster rate than agriculture, which was neglected by the Government. If the commodities are too dear, it is evident that we must turn our efforts towards agriculture. It is true that the task is difficult and alarming, for the young are drawn towards the towns by the high isalaries, amusements and shorter working days. It is absolutely impossible to find hands to work the land, the working hours are longer and the work is hard. The little money which the farmer puts by in the year, is due to his foresight, his economical way of living, and his long hours of labour. The farmers do not complain at all, they are happy and content with their lot. They only ask one thing from the city people: it is to cease their malevolent criticism. They do not blame the workmen for their day's work being shorter than their own. They do not begrudge them the few
dollars which they can spend' on amusements, for they understand that a man living in a city must need have recreation- They have no objection either to the workman eating oleomargarine if he wishes, provided1 this stuff does not sell for more than in other countries and is so marked that it may not be sold for butter.
It is said the farmer sells his produce too dear. The farmer does not go out of his way. It is the dealer who comes and offers him the price at which he sells his goods.
I can assure the hon. members on the otherside of the House who .live in cities, that if they paid for foodstuffs the price at which they are sold in the country, they would enjoy immediately a great decrease in the cost of living, and I can assure them at the same time that if the farmers sold their produce at the prices they sell for in the cities they would all he rich men. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, the middleman is the one to blame; and not only does he comer the goods, hut he allows them to spoil. In the city of Montreal alone, 366,000 pounds of meat and vegetables were confiscated last year.
Besides the farmer is himself a workman, a workman in the first, the largest of all industries, agriculture. The tillers of the soil, in the early days of the colony, were not only settlers, they were heroes; armed with an axe they pushed hack the forest, and armed with a gun they fought the enemy; not only did they succeed in broadening their land, they secured it to the British Crown; inch by inch they have brought it under cultivation and inch, by inch they have defended it. This soil on which they live to-day, bathed with the sweat of their brow, they love it, they are jealous for it. They know no other fatherland than Canada; they are in this country the true Canadians. I call the attention of the Government to that class of citizens. They are the only ones who can bring about our return to the days of peace.
The faults that bring blame upon the present Government are one of the principal causes of unrest in the country. The ministers resign one after the other; they change portfolios so often that even the members of this House have ceased to know who are the heads of the different departments. The right hon Prime Minister is at home everywhere but in Canada. No sooner does a vacancy occur in a desirable post than the hon. members, all conscious of the fact that they cannot be elected again, all turn greedy eyes towards it.

There is a talk of appointing a representative at Washington, and if we knew the secrets of the ministerial circles, we should be surprised at the stir and discontent which is caused by this coming appointment-The hon. President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) had been pointed to for this post; but the arrival of the Prime Minister seems to have unsettled the question. While on this side of the House we iare not made acquainted with the ministerial secrets, we fully surmise that there are more than two candidates for the position.
This Government have ceased to represent more than a part of the country. The interests of all the counties from Montreal to Halifax have been altogether ignored by them.
It would have ben a good policy this year to have fostered an -agricultural immigration to help the farmer, and also to have reduced -the duties on implements o-f production. Instead of taxing the people in order to procure a revenue, the Government might easily have adopted a policy tending to increase revenue through the development of our natural resources.
I think it is time, Mr. Speaker, that the Unionist tribe should bury the hatchet and that the hon. President of the Council should smoke the pipe of peace with his colleagues; I think it is time for us to cease talking war and to turn our attention towards cultivating good relations with our -allies, -and to the securing of a place in their markets.
I fear to weary yon, Mr. Speaker, hut I would also suggest to the ministers who have on various occasions to represent us in London, not to he content with abiding by the suggestions which they hear made to them, hut to affirm there as they do in this House, that Canada is a nation and that as such we have the right to he respected. I would ask them to affirm our royalty, but not to represent us as valets ready to do any bidding.
In order that the restoration of onr country may become an accomplished fact, Mr. Speaker, we need more unity between the different races ; it is absolutely necessary that all Canadians should join hands in the pursuit o-f the same ideal, that is to say make -a grand nation of this Canada of ours.
Mr. Speaker, as I said at the outset, I shall conclude my remarks in English. I thank you.
